investigacion.base:
As of the latest map, CONUS drought coverage is **about 2.8 points under the 58% threshold.** If the October 27 map came in at today's value, the question would resolve **Yes**.

**What the source says (USDM / Drought.gov)**
- **Latest value:** As of October 7, 2026, 46.29% of the United States and Puerto Rico and 55.21% of the Lower 48 states are in drought. This is the map released Thursday, October 8. USDM maps are dated each Tuesday, so its data-valid date is about October 6.
- **The week before:** Coverage was roughly 59%+. USDA's Brad Rippey said more than 59% of the contiguous United States was in drought at the end of September, and that coverage was virtually unchanged from the beginning of September through the week ending Sept. 29. So the latest map dropped about 4 points in one week, which is unusually large. (WeatherBug's "down 7%" probably refers to the U.S.+Puerto Rico figure or is a relative change.)
- **Where it changed:** Some of the biggest improvements occurred across portions of the West and areas west of the Plains. But drought worsened again across portions of Texas and Oklahoma, the Lower Midwest, Lower Mississippi River region and Southeast. Iowa is now nearly drought-free.
- I couldn't load the DataTables page itself, so the October 13 map (due out October 15) wasn't available to check.

**Context**
- The nation had passed the one-year mark of experiencing drought coverage exceeding 40% every week, a streak that began Sept. 16, 2025. September 2026 was the warmest on record for the contiguous U.S.
- **Outlooks:** CPC's October outlook favored drought improving or ending across part of the Southwest, Southern Plains, Southeast, and the Northeast. It gave the best odds of a dry October to the Northwest quadrant of the contiguous United States, stretching across the northern states from the Great Lakes westward to Washington and south through parts of California. The South is expected to be wetter, consistent with a strong El Niño. In Oregon, a state hydrologist expects no improvement this month because early October has been dry and warm.

**What's scheduled before resolution**
- October 13 map, released October 15
- October 20 map, released October 22
- October 27 map, released about October 29 (this one decides the question)

**Base rates**
Weekly changes in CONUS coverage are usually under 1–2 points. A 4-point drop like the latest one is uncommon. In autumn, drought often worsens during dry spells, but El Niño-driven rain in the South can cut coverage. For the question to resolve No, coverage would have to rise about 2.8 points or more across three maps. That's possible if the North and West stay dry and southern drought keeps getting worse, but it would mean reversing the recent improvement.

I didn't find any prediction-market prices for this question.

**Sources:**
- [1](https://www.drought.gov/national)
- [2](https://www.trentontelegraph.com/2026/10/12/news/h1-u-s-drought-coverage-remains-above-59-h1/)
- [3](https://weatherbug.com/news/Weekly%20Drought%20Conditions%20Update)
- [4](https://www.climate.us/news-features/understanding-climate/noaas-us-climate-outlook-october-2026)

criterios: This question resolves as **Yes** if, according to [U.S. Drought Monitor](https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/DmData/DataTables.aspx) for the data valid October 27, 2026, the contiguous United States (CONUS) has a cumulative percentage area of less than 58% classified  as D1 or worse (i.e., in the D1-D4 drought monitor categories).
letra_pequena: If no data valid for October 27, 2026 is released, the question resolves based on the first value released after that date.
razonamientos:
(a) **Time left:** The deciding map is valid October 27—13 days from today—and is expected to be released around October 29.

(b) **Status quo:** Yes. The latest reported Lower 48 drought coverage is 55.21%, about 2.8 percentage points below the threshold.

(c) **Reference class:** Over roughly three weekly Drought Monitor maps, a rise of nearly three percentage points is possible but not typical. I’d put its rough base rate around one in four; that is a judgment, not a measured historical frequency.

(d) **No scenario:** Continued dry weather expands drought across the North and West, while worsening conditions in Texas and the Southeast push coverage to at least 58%.

(e) **Yes scenario:** Recent improvements persist, or new drought develops too slowly to erase the current margin.

(f) **Resolution technicality:** The criterion is **D1–D4 coverage for CONUS**, not coverage including Puerto Rico or the D0 “abnormally dry” category. Exactly 58.00% resolves No. If no October 27 data is released, the first later value decides.

The current margin and short time remaining favor Yes, though the recent large weekly change shows the margin is not secure.

Probability: 77%

(c) **Reference class:** Three-week changes in autumn drought coverage. Weekly moves are usually under 1–2 percentage points; a rise of at least 2.79 points over three maps is plausible but not typical. I’d put its chance at roughly 20–30%, as a judgmental estimate rather than a measured historical base rate.

(d) **No scenario:** Dry weather expands drought in the North and West while conditions worsen in Texas or the Southeast, lifting coverage to at least 58%.

(e) **Yes scenario:** Coverage stays near its current level, or rain offsets drought expansion elsewhere.

Probability: 78%

(a) **Time left:** The deciding map is valid Tuesday, October 27, 2026, and should be released about October 29. That is roughly two weeks away, with three weekly maps still to come (Oct 13, Oct 20, Oct 27).

(b) **Status quo:** The latest reported CONUS D1–D4 coverage is 55.21%. That is about 2.8 points under the 58% threshold, so an unchanged value would resolve **Yes**.

(c) **Reference class:** Three-week changes in CONUS drought coverage. Weekly moves are usually under 1–2 points. A net rise of 2.8 points or more over three weeks happens perhaps 15–25% of the time during an active autumn flash-drought period. Rises are more likely after the warmest September on record, with dry outlooks for the North and West. Rises are less likely when El Niño is bringing rain to the South, which the October outlook favors.

(d) **No scenario:** The North and West stay dry and warm, as CPC favors. Drought keeps expanding in Texas, Oklahoma, the Lower Midwest, the Lower Mississippi and the Southeast. The forecast southern rains don't arrive, and coverage climbs back to about 58–59% or more.
- Separately, the 55.21% figure may be wrong. A source dated Oct 12 headlines coverage "remaining above 59%". It probably refers to late-September data, but it adds some uncertainty about the true current level.

(e) **Yes scenario:** The recent improvement in the West holds. El Niño-driven rain across the South trims drought in the Southwest, the Southern Plains and the Southeast. Coverage drifts within ±2 points of 55% and stays below 58%.

(f) **Technicalities:**
- October 27 is a Tuesday, so it matches a real USDM valid date.
- The measure is the CONUS cumulative D1–D4 percentage, not the U.S.-plus-Puerto Rico figure (46%). The 55.21% "Lower 48" number is the right comparison.
- The threshold is strictly "less than 58%".

The 2.8-point cushion and the wet-South outlook favor Yes. The dry North and West, the worsening southern pockets, and some doubt about the data keep meaningful No risk.

Probability: 74%
